mcqs.question: What is the key asymmetry in SSD flash storage that drives most of its unique behavior?
options: Reads are impossible without first performing a write
SSDs can only store data temporarily, unlike HDDs
Blocks and pages are always the same size on every SSD
You can read or write at small page granularity, but you can only erase at much larger block granularity, and a page must be erased before it can be rewritten
mcqs.explanation: The page-write, block-erase asymmetry is the root cause of write amplification, garbage collection, and wear leveling covered later in this topic. Reads don't require a prior write, SSDs are fully persistent storage, and block/page sizes vary by device — they're never equal in practice.

mcqs.question: Why can't an SSD simply overwrite a flash page with new data the way an HDD overwrites a sector?
options: SSD controllers are deliberately programmed to refuse overwrites for security reasons
SSDs have no concept of individually addressable pages at all
Overwriting is technically possible but disabled by default in all consumer drives
Flash physics only allow charge to move in one direction during a program operation; returning a page to a writable state requires erasing, which only happens at the larger block level
mcqs.explanation: The physical limitation is real and structural, not a policy choice: programming can only move cells toward one state, so returning to a writable state requires an erase, which is only possible at block granularity. This is why the controller must relocate data rather than overwrite in place.

mcqs.question: An application performs a 4KB logical write, but the SSD controller ends up physically writing 256KB to accomplish it. What is this ratio called, and why does it happen?
options: Write compression — the SSD is compressing data inefficiently
Write duplication — the SSD keeps two copies of all data by default
Write amplification — because modifying one page in a block with other valid pages can force a read-merge-erase-rewrite of the entire block
Write fragmentation — the file system split the write across many files
mcqs.explanation: Write amplification names exactly this ratio, and it occurs because erasing only works at block granularity — modifying one page in a block that has other still-valid pages can force relocating the whole block's worth of data. It has nothing to do with compression, deliberate duplication, or file fragmentation.

mcqs.question: Why would an SSD controller deliberately map the same logical address to a different physical block on each rewrite, rather than always writing to the same physical location?
options: It's a side effect of encryption and has no performance purpose
Wear leveling — spreading erase cycles evenly across the flash chip prevents one frequently-updated logical address from wearing out a single physical block long before the rest of the drive
It's required to support multiple file systems on one drive
It makes reads faster by fragmenting data across the chip
mcqs.explanation: This remapping, via the Flash Translation Layer, is specifically wear leveling: without it, a hot logical address (like a journal or WAL) would exhaust one physical block's limited erase-cycle budget far faster than the rest of the drive. It's unrelated to encryption, multi-filesystem support, or read performance via fragmentation.

mcqs.question: Why does an SSD need an explicit TRIM command, when an HDD never needed anything equivalent?
options: TRIM is purely a marketing feature with no real technical function
TRIM is required to make an SSD readable by the OS at all
HDDs actually do need an equivalent command, it's just rarely used

An HDD just overwrites whatever's physically there on the next write, regardless of what used to be there; an SSD's garbage collector needs to know a logical block is truly dead to avoid wastefully preserving it during reclamation
mcqs.explanation: HDDs have no concept of preserving 'still valid' data during a background process — the next write just overwrites in place. SSD garbage collection, by contrast, can waste real write cycles preserving data the file system has already marked deleted, unless TRIM explicitly signals that it's safe to discard. TRIM has a real, measurable performance effect, and SSDs work without it — just less efficiently over time.

mcqs.question: A team migrates a database from HDD to SSD storage but keeps their old HDD-tuned I/O scheduler and never issues TRIM. What's the most accurate assessment?
options: This is fine — SSDs are simply faster HDDs and need no configuration changes
They're leaving real performance and drive lifespan on the table — HDD-era scheduling assumptions and skipping TRIM both fail to account for how SSDs actually behave internally
The seek-minimizing scheduler will actively corrupt data on an SSD
TRIM only matters for HDDs, not SSDs
mcqs.explanation: SSDs and HDDs are genuinely different storage models, not just different speeds — seek-minimizing scheduling brings no benefit to SSDs, and skipping TRIM lets the SSD's garbage collector waste cycles preserving logically-dead data, hurting sustained write performance and wear. Neither issue causes data corruption, and TRIM is specifically an SSD concept, not an HDD one.
